newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH nibbles at Grand Met, seeks allies - analysts.
newsitem.headline: LVMH nibbles at Grand Met, seeks allies - analysts.

text.p: France's LVMH, stung by a renewed merger pledge between British drinks groups Guinness and Grand Metropolitan, confirmed on Tuesday that it had nudged up its stake in Grand Met to 6.3 percent.

The French luxury goods group declined to comment on its intentions, but industry sources and analysts expect it to keep amassing Grand Met shares unless the British companies agree to discuss LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault's alternative proposal.

LVMH, the biggest shareholder in Grand Met and Guinness, opposes their plan to merge into a sprawling giant worth more than 20 billion pounds ($33.4 billion) with activities ranging from Haagen-Dazs ice cream to Guinness stout and Green Giant canned vegetables.

Arnault, reputed in France for his tenacity and sharp business sense, wants to create a drinks group combining LVMH's Moet & Chandon and Hennessy brands with Guinness's Johnny Walker, Dewar's and Gordon's Gin labels and possibly Grand Met's Smirnoff, J&B and Baileys brands.

If LVMH raised its Grand Met stake to 10 percent, it could call an extraordinary general meeting of Grand Met shareholders. And if it lined up enough allies in the widely-held company to form a 25 percent block, it could stop the merger.
Most analysts say that appears to be LVMH's game plan.
"Arnault does not want to be marginalized in the drinks business," one Paris-based analyst said. He said Arnault looked to have won over a few fund managers.
LVMH, which built up a 6.29 percent stake in Grand Met last week, bought a further 250,000 shares, or 0.01 percent, at an average price of 587 pence, market sources said.
The next moves "depend on the reaction from Guinness and Grand Met. There are a lot of possibilities," an industry source said.

LVMH's own share price has slipped around three percent since it began buying Grand Met shares as investors worry that Arnault's strategy is expensive -- the Grand Met stake has cost LVMH eight billion francs ($1.4 billion) -- and carries risk. The stock was down 1.26 percent at 1,484 francs at midday on Tuesday.
"That's a lot of money to invest in a strategy that's not guaranteed to succeed," a portfolio manager said.
One analyst said LVMH's assault on Grand Met's capital suggested it may be less confident than it appeared on the strength of its legal case against Guinness.

LVMH threatened last month to buy Guinness out of their joint distribution ventures, which hold the rights to market Guinness brands in France, the United States and much of the Far East for 10 years.
It has asked the International Chamber of Commerce to uphold its right to exercise the options, which would shred the Grand Met-Guinness group's sales network, if the merger went ahead.
Guinness says LVMH has no right to exercise the options.

On Friday, responding to European and U.S. inquiries into possible antitrust implications of the merger, the two British companies reiterated in a joint statement that they expected the deal to close around the end of the year. Industry sources said the statement signalled a hardening of the positions.

Debt rating agency Standard & Poor's said on Friday it may downgrade LVMH's commercial paper rating, saying the company's inroads in Grand Met and the possible repurchase of Guinness's holdings in their ventures could stretch its finances.
LVMH paid $2.6 billion for control of U.S. chain Duty Free Shoppers in January and then sold a third of its Guinness stake for five billion francs, retaining 14.2 percent.
Its net debt is currently 12 billion francs on 36 billion francs of equity. ($ = 0.598 British Pounds) ($ = 5.818 French Francs)
